blocks.text: A car takes in fuel, gives out gas, moves, and even responds when you turn the key. Yet nobody calls a car alive. A tiny yeast cell in a sachet of baking powder does none of these things visibly, but it is alive. What exactly is the difference?

blocks.markdown:
## The seven life processes

An object is judged to be living if it shows **all** of the following. Showing only one or two is not enough — that is why a car and a candle flame do not qualify.

A useful mnemonic is **MR NIGER D**: Movement, Respiration, Nutrition, Irritability, Growth, Excretion, Reproduction, Death.

rows: Movement
A change in position of the whole organism or of its parts, brought about from within
A goat walking; a sunflower head turning towards the sun
Respiration
The release of energy from food inside living cells
Glucose broken down in the mitochondria of a muscle cell
Nutrition
Taking in or manufacturing food for energy, growth and repair
A maize plant photosynthesising; a person eating beans
Irritability (sensitivity)
Detecting and responding to a change in the surroundings, called a stimulus
A tilapia darting away from a shadow; a shoot bending towards light
Growth
A permanent increase in size, dry mass and complexity
A cassava cutting developing into a full plant
Excretion
Removing the waste products of metabolism from the body
Urea leaving the body in urine; carbon dioxide breathed out
Reproduction
Producing new individuals of the same kind
A hen laying fertile eggs; a yam tuber sprouting new plants
Death
All life processes eventually cease, and the body decays
A fallen mango leaf decomposing
blocks.caption: MR NIGER D — the characteristics of living things

blocks.title: Irritability
blocks.text: The ability of an organism to detect a stimulus and make an appropriate response. In animals this usually involves nerves and muscles; in plants it usually involves slow growth movements called tropisms.

blocks.markdown:
### Living, non-living, dead

Be careful with three different ideas.

- **Living** things carry out all seven processes now.
- **Dead** things once carried them out and have stopped. A dried plank of iroko wood is dead, not non-living.
- **Non-living** things never carried them out at all. A stone, a bottle of water, a plastic chair.

Some non-living objects mimic one or two life processes, which is why the full list matters. A river moves but does not respire. A crystal in a saturated solution grows, but only by adding identical layers on the outside, not by increasing in complexity, and it cannot reproduce or excrete.

blocks.title: Testing a doubtful case: is a virus alive?
blocks.prompt: Apply the characteristics of living things to a virus and decide whether a virus should be classified as living.

steps.text: Reproduction — a virus does reproduce, but only inside a living host cell, using the host's ribosomes and enzymes. It cannot reproduce on its own.
Nutrition and respiration — a virus has no cytoplasm, no mitochondria and no enzymes of its own, so it neither feeds nor respires.
Excretion and growth — with no metabolism there are no metabolic wastes to excrete, and a virus particle does not grow; it is assembled at full size.
Movement and irritability — a virus has no means of self-propelled movement and no way of responding to a stimulus. It drifts passively.
Weigh the evidence: it shows crystalline, non-living behaviour outside a host and living behaviour (reproduction, mutation) only inside one.

blocks.answer: A virus is best described as being on the borderline between living and non-living: it is an obligate parasite that shows only reproduction, and only inside a host cell. WAEC accepts 'shows characteristics of both living and non-living things'.

items: Plants move by slow growth responses (tropisms) rather than by locomotion, but this still counts as movement.
Excretion removes waste made by the body's own reactions; egestion removes undigested food that never entered the cells.
Growth in living things is irreversible and involves an increase in dry mass, not just in water content.
Respiration happens in every living cell all the time, whether or not the organism is breathing.

blocks.title: WAEC phrasing
blocks.text: When asked to distinguish living from non-living things, give characteristics in matched pairs and always include an example. A bare list of the seven words often scores only half the available marks.

points: Living things show movement, respiration, nutrition, irritability, growth, excretion, reproduction and eventually death.
An object must show all of these processes to be classed as living, not just one or two.
Dead things once carried out life processes; non-living things never did.
Excretion removes metabolic waste, while egestion removes undigested food.
Viruses lie on the borderline: they reproduce only inside a host cell and show no other life process.
